claim: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are the most common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are the most common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease (PD).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript referencing established literature on LRRK2 mutations and PD.

claim: DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice exhibit normal mortality.
source: Unlike Lrrk germline DKO mice, DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice exhibit normal mortality but develop age-dependent loss of DA neurons
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study comparing cDKO mice to germline DKO mice.

claim: DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice develop age-dependent loss of DA neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc).
source: Unlike Lrrk germline DKO mice, DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice exhibit normal mortality but develop age-dependent loss of DA neurons, as shown by the progressive reduction of DA neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) at the ages of 20 and 24 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data showing progressive reduction of DA neurons at 20 and 24 months.

claim: DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk cDKO mice is accompanied by increases in apoptosis in the SNpc.
source: Moreover, DA neurodegeneration is accompanied with increases in apoptosis and elevated microgliosis in the SNpc as well as decreases in DA terminals in the striatum
evidence: This is supported by active Caspase-3 immunostaining data showing increased apoptotic DA neurons.

claim: DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk cDKO mice is accompanied by elevated microgliosis in the SNpc.
source: Moreover, DA neurodegeneration is accompanied with increases in apoptosis and elevated microgliosis in the SNpc as well as decreases in DA terminals in the striatum
evidence: This is supported by Iba1 immunostaining data showing increased microglia in the SNpc.

claim: DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk cDKO mice is accompanied by decreases in DA terminals in the striatum.
source: Moreover, DA neurodegeneration is accompanied with increases in apoptosis and elevated microgliosis in the SNpc as well as decreases in DA terminals in the striatum
evidence: This is supported by TH immunoreactivity quantification in the striatum showing reduced levels at 24 months.

claim: DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk cDKO mice is preceded by impaired motor coordination.
source: Moreover, DA neurodegeneration is accompanied with increases in apoptosis and elevated microgliosis in the SNpc as well as decreases in DA terminals in the striatum, and is preceded by impaired motor coordination.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from beam walk tests showing motor deficits at 10 months before significant DA neuron loss.

claim: These findings provide unequivocal evidence for the cell-intrinsic requirement of LRRK in DA neurons.
source: Taken together, these findings provide the unequivocal evidence for the cell-intrinsic requirement of LRRK in DA neurons
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data from DA neuron-specific knockout mice showing cell-autonomous effects.

claim: LRRK2 mutations may impair its protection of DA neurons, leading to DA neurodegeneration in PD.
source: Taken together, these findings provide the unequivocal evidence for the cell-intrinsic requirement of LRRK in DA neurons and raise the possibility that LRRK2 mutations may impair its protection of DA neurons, leading to DA neurodegeneration in PD.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the loss-of-function data from the study.

claim: Dominantly inherited missense mutations in the leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (Lrrk2) gene are the most common cause of both familial and sporadic PD.
source: Dominantly inherited missense mutations in the leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (Lrrk2) gene are the most common cause of both familial and sporadic PD, highlighting the importance of LRRK2 in PD pathogenesis (Paisán-Ruíz et al., 2004; Shen, 2004; Zimprich et al., 2004; Gilks et al., 2005; Lesage et al., 2007; Kluss et al., 2019; Shu et al., 2019; Mata et al., 2005a; Mata et al., 2005b; Zabetian et al., 2005; Hatano et al., 2014; Takanashi et al., 2018; Nichols et al., 2005; Di Fonzo et al., 2005; Hernandez et al., 2005; Kachergus et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to published literature.

claim: LRRK2 is a large protein of 2527 amino acid residues containing multiple functional domains.
source: LRRK2 is a large protein of 2527 amino acid residues containing multiple functional domains, including several leucine-rich repeats (LRRs), a GTPase-like domain of Ras-of-complex (Roc), a C-terminal of Roc (COR) domain, and a serine/threonine MAPKKK-like kinase domain.
evidence: This is a description of the protein structure based on established knowledge.

claim: LRRK1 is a homolog of LRRK2 and belongs to the evolutionarily conserved Roco protein family.
source: LRRK1, a homolog of LRRK2, belongs to the evolutionarily conserved Roco protein family and contains similar LRRs, Roc, COR, and kinase domains (Bosgraaf and Van Haastert, 2003; Marín, 2006; Marín, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LRRK2 is most abundant in the kidney.
source: LRRK proteins are broadly expressed, with LRRK2 being most abundant in the kidney (Biskup et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Rare variants in the Roc, COR, and kinase domains of LRRK1 have been reported and may be associated with PD.
source: While most PD mutations are found in LRRK2, rare variants in the Roc, COR, and kinase domains of LRRK1 have been reported and may be associated with PD (Schulte et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Roc-COR domain of LRRK2 forms dimers and exhibits conventional Ras-like GTPase properties.
source: Furthermore, the Roc-COR domain of LRRK2 forms dimers and exhibits conventional Ras-like GTPase properties, and the R1441/C/G/H and I1371V mutations destabilize dimer formation and decrease GTPase activity (Deng et al., 2008; Mills et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: R1441/C/G/H and I1371V mutations destabilize dimer formation and decrease GTPase activity.
source: Furthermore, the Roc-COR domain of LRRK2 forms dimers and exhibits conventional Ras-like GTPase properties, and the R1441/C/G/H and I1371V mutations destabilize dimer formation and decrease GTPase activity (Deng et al., 2008; Mills et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High-resolution cryoEM structural studies demonstrated LRRK2 exists as dimers.
source: Recent high-resolution cryoEM structural studies of full-length LRRK2 demonstrated its existence as dimers and pathogenic mutations such as R1441/C/G/H and Y1699I at the Roc-COR interface, whereas the G2910S mutant is structurally similar to the wild-type LRRK2 (Myasnikov et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LRRK2 plays essential roles in the autophagy-lysosomal pathway.
source: Previous genetic studies demonstrated that LRRK2 plays essential roles in the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (Tong et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lrrk2-/- mice develop age-dependent phenotypes in the kidney, including autophagy-lysosomal impairments and increases in α-synuclein, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses.
source: Consistent with high levels of LRRK2 expression in kidneys, Lrrk2-/- mice develop age-dependent phenotypes in the kidney, including autophagy-lysosomal impairments and increases in α-synuclein, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses (Tong et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2012; Tong and Shen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LRRK2 is important for maintaining lung homeostasis.
source: It has also been reported that LRRK2 is important for maintaining lung homeostasis, and Lrrk2 deficiency results in impaired autophagy in alveolar type II epithelial cells (Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Lrrk2 deficiency results in impaired autophagy in alveolar type II epithelial cells.
source: It has also been reported that LRRK2 is important for maintaining lung homeostasis, and Lrrk2 deficiency results in impaired autophagy in alveolar type II epithelial cells (Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The lack of brain phenotypes in Lrrk2-/- mice might be due to the presence of LRRK1, which could compensate functionally in the absence of LRRK2.
source: It was proposed that the lack of brain phenotypes in Lrrk2-/- mice might be due to the presence of LRRK1, which could compensate functionally in the absence of LRRK2 (Tong et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Lrrk double knockout (DKO) mice develop an age-dependent, progressive loss of DA neurons in the SNpc, beginning at 14 months of age.
source: Indeed, Lrrk double knockout (DKO) mice develop an age-dependent, progressive loss of DA neurons in the SNpc, beginning at 14 months of age (Giaime et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Lrrk DKO mice exhibit lower body weight and earlier mortality.
source: However, Lrrk DKO mice also exhibit lower body weight and earlier mortality, raising the possibility that DA neurodegeneration in aged Lrrk germline DKO mice may be secondary to poor health.
evidence: This is an observation from previous studies, supported by citation and inference.

claim: DA neurodegeneration in aged Lrrk germline DKO mice may be secondary to poor health.
source: However, Lrrk DKO mice also exhibit lower body weight and earlier mortality, raising the possibility that DA neurodegeneration in aged Lrrk germline DKO mice may be secondary to poor health.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observations from previous studies.

claim: Cre recombinase is expressed under the control of the endogenous promoter of the dopamine transporter gene Slc6a3 in Slc6a3-Cre knockin (KI) mice.
source: In this study, we investigate whether LRRK2 and its functional homolog LRRK1 play an essential, intrinsic role in DA neurons through the development of DA neuron-specific Lrrk conditional DKO (cDKO) mice using the Slc6a3-Cre knockin (KI) allele, in which Cre recombinase is expressed under the control of the endogenous promoter of the dopamine transporter gene Slc6a3.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic tool used in the study.

claim: Floxed Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 mice were generated and confirmed.
source: We first generated and confirmed floxed Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 mice, and then crossed them with the CMV-Cre deleter to create germline deletions of the floxed Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 alleles
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Northern and western analyses confirmed the absence of Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 mRNAs, as well as LRRK1 and LRRK2 proteins in the respective homozygous deleted mutant mice.
source: We first generated and confirmed floxed Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 mice, and then crossed them with the CMV-Cre deleter to create germline deletions of the floxed Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 alleles, followed by northern and western analyses to confirm the absence of Lrrk1 and Lrrk2 mRNAs, as well as LRRK1 and LRRK2 proteins in the respective homozygous deleted mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by northern and western blot data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination occurs in most, if not all, DA neurons in the SNpc and is restricted to DA neurons.
source: We also crossed a GFP reporter mouse with Slc6a3-Cre KI mice and confirmed that Cre-mediated recombination occurs in most, if not all, DA neurons in the SNpc and is restricted to DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data showing 99% of TH+ neurons are also GFP+.

claim: DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice of both sexes exhibit normal mortality and body weight.
source: While DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice of both sexes exhibit normal mortality and body weight, they develop age-dependent loss of DA neurons in the SNpc
evidence: This is supported by body weight and survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The progressive reduction of TH+ DA neurons or NeuN+ neurons in the SNpc of cDKO mice occurs at the ages of 20 and 24 months but not at 15 months.
source: While DA neuron-restricted Lrrk cDKO mice of both sexes exhibit normal mortality and body weight, they develop age-dependent loss of DA neurons in the SNpc, as demonstrated by the progressive reduction of TH+ DA neurons or NeuN+ neurons in the SNpc of cDKO mice at the ages of 20 and 24 months but not at 15 months.
evidence: This is supported by stereological quantification data of TH+ and NeuN+ neurons.

claim: Quantitative electron microscopy (EM) analysis showed a similar number of electron-dense vacuoles in SNpc neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice relative to controls.
source: Interestingly, quantitative electron microscopy (EM) analysis showed a similar number of electron-dense vacuoles in SNpc neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice relative to controls, in contrast to age-dependent increases in vacuoles in SNpc neurons of Lrrk germline DKO mice (Giaime et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by EM quantification data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Age-dependent increases in vacuoles occur in SNpc neurons of Lrrk germline DKO mice.
source: Interestingly, quantitative electron microscopy (EM) analysis showed a similar number of electron-dense vacuoles in SNpc neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice relative to controls, in contrast to age-dependent increases in vacuoles in SNpc neurons of Lrrk germline DKO mice (Giaime et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 99% of TH+ DA neurons in the SNpc are also GFP+ in Slc6a3Cre/+; Rosa26CAG-LSL-ZsGreen1/+ mice.
source: Quantification of GFP+ and/or TH+ cells in the SNpc showed that 99% of TH+ DA neurons are also GFP+, demonstrating that Cre-mediated recombination takes place in essentially all DA neurons in the SNpc (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice and littermate controls have similar body and brain weights at the ages of 2–24 months.
source: However, DA neuron-specific Lrrk cDKO and littermate control mice have similar body and brain weights at the ages of 2–24 months (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by body and brain weight measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Western analysis showed a significant reduction of LRRK1 and LRRK2 proteins in the dissected ventral midbrain but not in the cerebral cortex of DA neuron-specific Lrrk cDKO mice at 2–3 months of age.
source: Western analysis showed a significant reduction of LRRK1 and LRRK2 proteins in the dissected ventral midbrain but not in the cerebral cortex of DA neuron-specific Lrrk cDKO mice at 2–3 months of age, relative to littermate controls (Figure 2E and F)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The morphology of TH+ DA neurons in Lrrk cDKO mice at the ages of 15, 20, and 24 months appears normal.
source: The morphology of TH+ DA neurons in Lrrk cDKO mice at the ages of 15, 20, and 24 months appears normal (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The number of DA neurons in the SNpc at the age of 15 months is similar between cDKO mice (10,000 ± 141) and littermate controls (10,077 ± 310).
source: Quantification of TH+ neurons in the SNpc using serial sections emcompassing the entire SNpc revealed that the number of DA neurons in the SNpc at the age of 15 months is similar between cDKO mice (10,000 ± 141) and littermate controls (10,077 ± 310; F1,46 = 16.59, p=0.0002, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni's post hoc multiple comparisons, p>0.9999; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At the age of 20 months, the number of TH+ neurons in the SNpc of cDKO mice (8948 ± 273) is significantly reduced compared to controls (10,244 ± 220).
source: However, at the age of 20 months, the number of TH+ neurons in the SNpc of cDKO mice (8948 ± 273) is significantly reduced compared to controls (10,244 ± 220; p=0.0041)
evidence: This is supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At the age of 24 months, the number of TH+ neurons in the SNpc of cDKO mice (8188 ± 452) is significantly reduced compared to controls (9675 ± 232).
source: and is further decreased at the age of 24 months (control: 9675 ± 232, cDKO: 8188 ± 452; p=0.0010; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The number of NeuN+ neurons in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice (17,923 ± 813) at 24 months is significantly lower than that in control mice (21,907 ± 469).
source: Quantification of NeuN+ cells in the SNpc shows that the number of NeuN+ neurons in Lrrk cDKO mice (17,923 ± 813) is significantly lower than that in control mice (21,907 ± 469, p=0.0006, Student's t-test), indicating loss of neurons in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from NeuN immunostaining shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The number of TH+/NeuN+ cells in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice (10,500 ± 644) at 24 months is lower compared to control mice (14,102 ± 310).
source: The number of TH+/NeuN+ cells in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice (10,500 ± 644) is also lower compared to control mice (14,102 ± 310, p=0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from double immunostaining shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is no significant difference in the number of NeuN+/TH- neurons between littermate controls (7804 ± 249) and cDKO mice (7423 ± 344) at 24 months.
source: There is no significant difference in the number of NeuN+/TH- neurons between littermate controls (7804 ± 249) and cDKO mice (7423 ± 344, p=0.3747).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduction in TH+ cells is not due to decreases in TH expression in DA neurons, but rather a result of the loss of DA neuron cell bodies in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice.
source: These data indicate that the reduction in TH+ cells is not due to decreases in TH expression in DA neurons, but rather a result of the loss of DA neuron cell bodies in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the NeuN and TH double staining data.

claim: Quantification of active Caspase-3+/TH+ apoptotic DA neurons shows a significant increase in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice (323 ± 38) at 24 months compared to controls (157 ± 8).
source: Quantification of active Caspase-3+/TH+ apoptotic DA neurons shows a significant increase in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice (323 ± 38) compared to controls (157 ± 8, p=0.0004, Student's t-test; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from active Caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LRRK plays an intrinsic role in the survival of DA neurons in the SNpc during aging.
source: These results further support that LRRK plays an intrinsic role in the survival of DA neurons in the SNpc during aging.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the apoptosis data.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice show normal levels of TH immunoreactivity in the striatum at 15 months of age.
source: Quantitative analysis showed normal levels of TH immunoreactivity in the striatum of cDKO mice at 15 months of age
evidence: This is supported by TH immunoreactivity quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice show reduced levels of TH immunoreactivity in the striatum at 24 months of age (–19%).
source: but reduced levels of TH immunoreactivity in the striatum of cDKO mice at 24 moths of age (–19%, p=0.0215, Student's t-test), suggesting an age-dependent loss of TH+ dopaminergic terminals in the striatum (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by TH immunoreactivity quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is an age-dependent loss of TH+ dopaminergic terminals in the striatum of Lrrk cDKO mice.
source: but reduced levels of TH immunoreactivity in the striatum of cDKO mice at 24 moths of age (–19%, p=0.0215, Student's t-test), suggesting an age-dependent loss of TH+ dopaminergic terminals in the striatum (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TH immunoreactivity data.

claim: The number of TH+ cells in the LC is similar between cDKO and littermate controls at 24 months (control: 3418 ± 86, cDKO: 3350 ± 99).
source: The number of TH+ cells in the LC is similar between cDKO and littermate controls (control: 3418 ± 86, cDKO: 3350 ± 99, p=0.6110, Student's t-test; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from TH immunostaining in the LC shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is a lack of Cre-mediated recombination in the LC of Slc6a3Cre/+ mice.
source: Further examination of the GFP reporter line crossed with Slc6a3Cre/+ showed the lack of Cre-mediated recombination in the LC (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lack of Cre-mediated recombination in the LC supports the cell-intrinsic nature of DA neuron loss in the SNpc of aged Lrrk cDKO mice.
source: Further examination of the GFP reporter line crossed with Slc6a3Cre/+ showed the lack of Cre-mediated recombination in the LC (Figure 6C), supporting the cell-intrinsic nature of DA neuron loss in the SNpc of aged Lrrk cDKO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the GFP reporter data.

claim: The number of electron-dense vacuoles in the SNpc is similar between Lrrk cDKO mice and littermate controls at the age of 25 months (control: 6.72 ± 0.43, cDKO: 6.99 ± 0.52).
source: Interestingly, the number of electron-dense vacuoles in the SNpc is similar between Lrrk cDKO mice and littermate controls at the age of 25 months (control: 6.72 ± 0.43, cDKO: 6.99 ± 0.52, p=0.6839, Student's t-test; Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by EM quantification data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: There is no significant difference in the area of electron-dense vacuoles in the SNpc between Lrrk cDKO and littermate controls at 25 months (control: 4.43 ± 0.44 μm2; cDKO: 4.60 ± 0.49 μm2).
source: We also found no significant difference in the area of electron-dense vacuoles in the SNpc between Lrrk cDKO and littermate controls (control: 4.43 ± 0.44 μm2; cDKO: 4.60 ± 0.49 μm2, p=0.8048; Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by EM quantification data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: LRRK in non-DA neurons, possibly microglia, may play a more prominent role in the regulation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway.
source: The difference in accumulation of electron-dense vacuoles in the SNpc between germline DKO mice and DA neuron-restricted cDKO suggests that LRRK in non-DA neurons, possibly microglia, may play a more prominent role in the regulation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the difference in EM findings between germline DKO and cDKO mice.

claim: The number of Iba1+ microglia is significantly increased in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice at 15 months of age (2541 ± 193), compared to controls (1737 ± 83).
source: We found that the number of Iba1+ microglia is significantly increased in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice at 15 months of age (2541 ± 193), compared to controls (1737 ± 83; F1,45 = 102.6, p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni's post hoc multiple comparisons, p=0.0017; Figure 8A and D).
evidence: This is supported by Iba1 immunostaining quantification data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The number of Iba1+ microglia in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO is further increased compared to controls at the age of 20 months (control: 2426 ± 68, cDKO: 3639 ± 127).
source: The number of Iba1+ microglia in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO is further increased compared to controls at the age of 20 (control: 2426 ± 68, cDKO: 3639 ± 127, p<0.0001; Figure 8B and D)
evidence: This is supported by Iba1 immunostaining quantification data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The number of Iba1+ microglia in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO is further increased compared to controls at the age of 25 months (control: 2640 ± 187, cDKO: 4089 ± 100).
source: and 25 months (control: 2640 ± 187, cDKO: 4089 ± 100, p<0.0001; Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Iba1 immunostaining quantification data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Microgliosis is elevated in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice, even though LRRK expression in microglia is unaffected in these mice.
source: These results show that despite the selective inactivation of LRRK in DA neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice, microgliosis accompanies DA neuronal loss in the SNpc.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the microgliosis data in DA neuron-specific knockout mice.

claim: Microgliosis in Lrrk cDKO mice suggests a cell-extrinsic microglial response to pathophysiological changes in DA neurons.
source: Furthermore, microgliosis is elevated in the SNpc of Lrrk cDKO mice, even though LRRK expression in microglia is unaffected in these mice, suggesting a cell-extrinsic microglial response to pathophysiological changes in DA neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the microgliosis data.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age displayed significantly more hindlimb slips/errors (4.4 ± 0.5) in the 10 mm beam walk test, relative to littermate controls (2.0 ± 0.3).
source: Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age displayed significantly more hindlimb slips/errors (4.4 ± 0.5) and longer traversal time (7.3 ± 0.3) in the 10 mm beam walk test, relative to littermate controls, which exhibited fewer slips (2.0 ± 0.3, p=0.0005, Student's t-test)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age displayed longer traversal time (7.3 ± 0.3) in the 10 mm beam walk test, relative to littermate controls (5.8 ± 0.4).
source: Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age displayed significantly more hindlimb slips/errors (4.4 ± 0.5) and longer traversal time (7.3 ± 0.3) in the 10 mm beam walk test, relative to littermate controls, which exhibited fewer slips (2.0 ± 0.3, p=0.0005, Student's t-test) and shorter traversal time (5.8 ± 0.4, p=0.0075; Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the 20 mm beam walk, both Lrrk cDKO (1.5 ± 0.2) and littermate controls (1.0 ± 0.2) at 10 months of age performed well with few hindlimb slips and with no difference between Lrrk cDKO and control mice.
source: In the 20 mm beam walk, which is less challenging than the narrower beam walk, both Lrrk cDKO (1.5 ± 0.2) and littermate controls (1.0 ± 0.2, p=0.0733) at 10 months of age performed well with few hindlimb slips and with no difference between Lrrk cDKO and control mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The traversal time in the 20 mm beam walk is similar between Lrrk cDKO (5.2 ± 0.3) and control littermates (5.1 ± 0.4) at 10 months.
source: In addition, the traversal time is similar between Lrrk cDKO (5.2 ± 0.3) and control littermates (5.1 ± 0.4, p=0.9796; Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age exhibit deficits in motor coordination.
source: These results show that Lrrk cDKO mice at 10 months of age already exhibit deficits in motor coordination.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the beam walk test data.

claim: In the pole test, Lrrk cDKO and control mice at 10 months showed similar turning time (control: 1.2 ± 0.1; cDKO: 1.5 ± 0.1) and descending time (control: 4.7 ± 0.1; cDKO: 4.7 ± 0.2).
source: However, in the pole test Lrrk cDKO and control mice showed similar turning time (control: 1.2 ± 0.1; cDKO: 1.5 ± 0.1; p=0.1219) and descending time (control: 4.7 ± 0.1; cDKO: 4.7 ± 0.2; p=0.8620; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the pole test shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Lrrk cDKO and control mice at 10 months of age exhibit similar body weight.
source: The Lrrk cDKO and control mice at 10 months of age exhibit similar body weight (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Aged Lrrk cDKO and control mice at 22 months performed similarly in hindlimb errors and traversal time in 10 mm beam walk test.
source: The aged Lrrk cDKO and control mice performed similarly in hindlimb errors (p=0.7022) and traversal time (p=0.8139) in 10 mm beam walk test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The hindlimb slips and traversal time of both genotypic groups at 22 months were much higher compared to the respective groups of younger mice.
source: The hindlimb slips (control: 12.0 ± 3.0; cDKO: 13.8 ± 3.3) and traversal time (control: 15.3 ± 2.0; cDKO: 16.2 ± 2.8) of both genotypic groups were much higher compared to the respective groups of younger mice (p<0.0001; Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the beam walk test shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Higher percentage of the aged mice (2–3 out of 8–9 per genotypic group) failed the beam walk test compared to the younger mice (0–2 mice out of 18–20 per genotypic group).
source: Moreover, higher percentage of the aged mice (2–3 out of 8–9 per genotypic group) failed the test compared to the younger mice (0–2 mice out of 18–20 per genotypic group, Figure 9A and D).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 9A and D.

claim: Aged mice of both genotypes perform poorly in the challenging narrow beam walk test.
source: These results show that aged mice of both genotypes perform poorly in the challenging narrow beam walk test, suggesting that it is not optimal to reveal subtle differences in motor coordination between the genotypic groups at this age.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the behavioral data at 22 months.

claim: The narrow beam walk test is not optimal to reveal subtle differences in motor coordination between the genotypic groups at 22 months of age.
source: These results show that aged mice of both genotypes perform poorly in the challenging narrow beam walk test, suggesting that it is not optimal to reveal subtle differences in motor coordination between the genotypic groups at this age.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the behavioral data.

claim: The pleiotropic roles of LRRK1 and LRRK2 in the kidney, lung, and bone, and the observed earlier mortality and lower body weight in Lrrk DKO mice raised the possibility that DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk DKO mice may be due to poor health.
source: However, the pleiotropic roles of LRRK1 and LRRK2 in the kidney (Tong et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2012; Tong and Shen, 2012), lung (Tian et al., 2021), and bone (Xing et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2017), and the observed earlier mortality and lower body weight in Lrrk DKO mice raised the possibility that DA neurodegeneration in Lrrk DKO mice may be due to poor health.

claim: The molecular mechanism by which LRRK supports cell-autonomous DA neuron survival is unknown.
source: The molecular mechanism by which LRRK supports cell-autonomous DA neuron survival is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a gap in knowledge.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing of dissected ventral midbrains may permit identification of genes and pathways that are selectively altered in DA neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice before and after the onset of DA neurodegeneration.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing of dissected ventral midbrains may permit identification of genes and pathways that are selectively altered in DA neurons of Lrrk cDKO mice before and after the onset of DA neurodegeneration.

source: Development of microglia- and/or astrocyte-specific Lrrk cDKO mice would permit further dissection of cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous roles of LRRK in DA neuron survival and determine whether glial LRRK plays a more important role in the regulation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and protein turnover.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research.

source: It would also be interesting to test whether reducing LRRK expression or function affects accumulation and aggregation of human mutant α-synuclein and tau in the aging brain, as both Lewy bodies and tauopathies are associated with PD patients carrying LRRK2 mutations (Zimprich et al., 2004).

source: It would also be interesting to test whether reducing LRRK expression or function affects accumulation and aggregation of human mutant α-synuclein and tau in the aging brain, as both Lewy bodies and tauopathies are associated with PD patients carrying LRRK2 mutations (Zimprich et al., 2004).

claim: The toxic gain-of-function pathogenic mechanism was initially proposed based on in vitro kinase assays using recombinant mutant LRRK2, which showed that R1441C and G2019S resulted in increases in autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of a generic substrate.
source: The toxic gain-of-function pathogenic mechanism was initially proposed based on in vitro kinase assays using recombinant mutant LRRK2, which showed that R1441C and G2019S resulted in increases in autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of a generic substrate (West et al., 2005).

claim: LRRK2 mutations (e.g., R1441C/G, G2019S) enhanced kinase activity, leading to elevated levels of pSer1292-LRRK2 as well as pT73-Rab10 and pS106-Rab12.
source: Subsequent biochemical studies further reported that LRRK2 mutations (e.g., R1441C/G, G2019S) enhanced kinase activity, leading to elevated levels of pSer1292-LRRK2 (Sheng et al., 2012) as well as pT73-Rab10 and pS106-Rab12 (Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: While these biochemical changes are excellent biomarkers of LRRK2 mutations, there is no experimental evidence showing that increased phosphorylation of LRRK2 substrates drives DA neurodegeneration.
source: While these biochemical changes are excellent biomarkers of LRRK2 mutations, there is no experimental evidence showing that increased phosphorylation of LRRK2 substrates drives DA neurodegeneration.

claim: The loss-of-function pathogenic mechanism was prompted by mouse knockout findings showing that germline inactivation of the Lrrk genes results in age-dependent loss of DA neurons in the SNpc and DA terminals in the striatum.
source: The loss-of-function pathogenic mechanism was prompted by mouse knockout findings showing that germline inactivation of the Lrrk genes results in age-dependent loss of DA neurons in the SNpc and DA terminals in the striatum (Giaime et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The current study demonstrated a cell-intrinsic role of LRRK in support of DA neuron survival in the SNpc of the aging brain.
source: The current study demonstrated a cell-intrinsic role of LRRK in support of DA neuron survival in the SNpc of the aging brain, providing an unequivocal genetic evidence of an essential, cell-autonomous requirement of LRRK in DA neurons.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Most transgenic mice overexpressing mutant LRRK2 did not produce neurodegeneration or DA neuron loss.
source: While most transgenic mice overexpressing mutant LRRK2 did not produce neurodegeneration or DA neuron loss (Li et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Melrose et al., 2010; Daher et al., 2012; Tsika et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Mikhail et al., 2015; Xiong et al., 2017)

source: Two reports of genomic database analysis suggested that loss-of-function Lrrk2 and Lrrk1 variants are not associated with PD (Whiffin et al., 2020; Blauwendraat et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One study was a predictive analysis using several available sequencing databases, and the authors cautiously stated that heterozygous predicted loss-of-function variants are not strongly associated with PD.
source: One study was a predictive analysis using several available sequencing databases (141,456 individuals sequenced in the Genome Aggregation Database, 49,960 exome-sequenced individuals from the UK Biobank, and more than 4 million participants in the 23andMe genotyped dataset), and the authors cautiously stated that heterozygous predicted loss-of-function variants are not strongly associated with PD (Whiffin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Another study analyzed next-generation sequencing data from 11,095 PD patients and 12,615 controls, and found that Lrrk1 loss-of-function variants were identified in 0.205% PD cases and 0.139% of controls, whereas Lrrk2 loss-of-function variants were found in 0.117% of PD cases and 0.087% of controls.
source: Another study analyzed next-generation sequencing data from 11,095 PD patients and 12,615 controls, and found that Lrrk1 loss-of-function variants were identified in 0.205% PD cases and 0.139% of controls, whereas Lrrk2 loss-of-function variants were found in 0.117% of PD cases and 0.087% of controls (Blauwendraat et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: These genomic database analysis studies are considerably weaker with the results suggestive but highly inconclusive.

claim: It is quite possible that haploinsufficiency or heterozygous complete loss-of-function mutations are not sufficient to cause the disease; rather a dominant negative mechanism, coupled with loss of function missense mutations, may be at play.
source: Moreover, it is quite possible that haploinsufficiency or heterozygous complete loss-of-function mutations are not sufficient to cause the disease; rather a dominant negative mechanism, coupled with loss of function missense mutations, may be at play, reducing overall protein function further, especially if dimers are the functional entities.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the pathogenic mechanism.

claim: These studies are interesting but inconclusive as to whether loss-of-function mutations in LRRK2 or LRRK1 cause or do not cause PD.
source: Therefore, these studies are interesting but inconclusive as to whether loss-of-function mutations in LRRK2 or LRRK1 cause or do not cause PD.

source: Missense mutations in the PSEN genes linked to familial Alzheimer's disease are good examples of such a loss-of-function coupled with a dominant negative mechanism (Shen and Kelleher, 2007; Heilig et al., 2010; Heilig et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2017; Watanabe and Shen, 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Kelleher and Shen, 2017).
